Neonatal specimens of Emydocephalus ijimae emerge from parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length averaging 28 centimeters [Lb = 28 centimeters], a size that positions this sea snake among the larger-bodied hydrophiines at birth. The hatchlings, which undergo eclosion after a developmental incubation period of approximately 183 days [ab = approximately 183 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant 24 °C [T = 24 °C], emerge as fully independent, lecithotrophic neonates with no residual yolk sac to absorb. This prolonged incubation at 24 °C [T = 24 °C] reflects the thermosensitive nature of embryonic development in oviparous marine reptiles, where lower thermal regimes typically extend the duration of embryogenesis. The considerable size at hatching likely confers a survival advantage in the predator-rich coral reef habitats these young snakes must navigate, enabling them to forage on small fish eggs and newly hatched prey items almost immediately after emergence. Field measurements of wild-born neonates consistently fall between 226 and 342 millimeters (226 to 342 millimeters) [Lb = 226 to 342 millimeters], indicating a degree of phenotypic plasticity influenced by maternal provisioning and intra-clutch variation in egg size. This birth length represents a substantial proportion of adult dimensions, suggesting a relatively rapid growth trajectory in the early postnatal period.

Males of Emydocephalus ijimae attain puberty, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and functional reproductive capability, at a snout-vent length of 55 centimeters [Lp = 55 centimeters], a size typically reached within their second or third year of life. Females, by contrast, initiate gonadal activation and become capable of producing their first clutch at a slightly smaller body size of 50 centimeters [Lp = 50 centimeters], reflecting a sexual dimorphism in maturation thresholds that is common among oviparous elapids. The difference in size at puberty between the sexes is modest, amounting to only five centimeters, but it implies that males must invest additional growth before their reproductive activation can proceed. This pattern contrasts with many terrestrial snakes, where females often mature at larger sizes; the reversed trend in this marine specialist may be linked to the energetic demands of egg production in a thermally stable but resource-limited environment. Upon reaching sexual maturation, individuals begin to allocate resources toward cloacal copulation and internal fertilisation, with sperm storage likely occurring in females to facilitate asynchronous mating events. The relatively small size differential between the sexes at maturity suggests that both males and females experience similar growth constraints during their juvenile phase, a period characterised by active foraging and avoidance of predators such as sharks and larger teleost fishes.

The ultimate snout-vent length attained by reproductively active adult females of Emydocephalus ijimae reaches 85.5 centimeters [Li = 85.5 centimeters], a measurement that represents the asymptotic body size for this sex. Males, in contrast, achieve a smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 78.5 centimeters [Li = 78.5 centimeters], a disparity that reflects the broader sexual size dimorphism evident in this oviparous hydrophiine. This substantial mass difference—females are nearly 65 percent heavier than males at their asymptotic size—is likely driven by the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and the production of multiple yolk-laden eggs per clutch. The larger body size of females may also confer a fecundity advantage, allowing them to accommodate a greater number of developing follicles within the coelomic cavity. Observations of free-ranging populations suggest that females continue to grow slowly even after reaching reproductive maturity, whereas males appear to approach their asymptotic size more rapidly and plateau earlier in life.

Females do not appear to store sperm from a single copulation to fertilize multiple clutches, instead engaging in new reproductive pairings prior to each oviposition event. The combination of one clutch per year and two to six eggs per clutch suggests that total annual egg output is relatively low, placing this species toward the slow end of the life-history continuum for sea snakes. This strategy presumably reflects the high per-offspring investment required to produce large, independent young capable of immediate foraging in coral reef ecosystems.

Maximum lifespan records for Emydocephalus ijimae, derived from long-term mark-recapture studies in the Ryukyu Archipelago and supplemented by captive observations at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], indicate that these snakes can survive for up to 20 years [am = up to 20 years] under natural conditions. Comparative data from related Hydrophiinae species suggest that the lifespan of Emydocephalus ijimae is among the highest recorded for sea snakes, with senescence becoming apparent only after the fifteenth year in most individuals. The coupling of delayed maturation, modest annual fecundity, and exceptional longevity positions this species as a classic example of a slow-paced life-history strategy in a thermally stable marine environment.
